Triggers.value: Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
I have to be on guard all the time
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

issues.explanation: The trigger set mixes a socially evaluative trigger ('being seen') with nonspecific discomfort/detachment, while the threat items center on danger from sudden sounds, home intrusion, and interpersonal harm. For a combat trauma profile, 'being seen' is not impossible, but here it is poorly linked to the stated threat pattern and stands out as the one trigger not plausibly connected to the strong Triggers→Threat and Triggers→Negative Appraisals edges.

issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: Within Threat, hypervigilance to loud sounds and watching others for danger fit a combat-related threat profile, but specifically monitoring for someone entering the home implies a domestic intrusion threat context that is not supported by the triggers, memory, or appraisals. It pulls the profile toward a different trauma context and weakens cross-node coherence.

vignette:
Marcus had served for years as a park ranger, a job that suited his steady manner and his familiarity with long stretches of quiet, but there had been a night in combat overseas that divided his life into before and after. During an operation in a hostile area, he had been part of a small unit moving through a tight stretch of ground when helicopters came in overhead and the sound of aircraft filled the air. What should have felt like support instead became part of the terror of the moment, because the noise was loud, unexpected, and impossible to ignore while he and the others were trying to make sense of what was happening around them. Marcus still described that night with unusual precision, as if the details had been stamped into him: the feeling of being on edge before anything even happened, the harsh mechanical sound above him, and the way the event seemed to carry a smell he could still sometimes catch in memory, bringing the whole scene back with a force that ordinary recollections did not have. Even years later, he said those memories felt more real and vivid than memories of normal days, as though the event had been preserved in sharper focus than the rest of his life.

After returning home, Marcus found that certain sounds could pull him back into that state immediately. Helicopters passing over the ranger station, aircraft overhead, or any sudden loud noise could make him feel as if he was back in the line of danger before he had time to think. He would tense, go still, and begin to feel detached, almost unreal, as though the world had taken on a thin, distant quality. At work, if a helicopter crossed above the trees or came near the park, he would interrupt what he was doing and look up sharply, his attention narrowing to the sound. He was not able to dismiss it as background noise; his body treated it as a warning. The same was true when a door banged or a branch cracked unexpectedly. He became alert in an instant, listening hard, watching for the source, and taking in everything around him with a level of intensity that left little room for ease.

Over time, Marcus developed the habit of constantly scanning his surroundings for danger. On patrol, he watched visitors, hikers, and unfamiliar vehicles closely, searching people's faces and movements for any sign that someone might mean harm. In the park office, in the visitor areas, and even in ordinary public places with his wife, he seemed to be studying the environment rather than simply moving through it. His wife noticed that he checked exits, looked over his shoulder, and rarely let himself settle fully. Marcus himself explained it in terms of responsibility, saying he had to be on guard all the time. He had come to believe that if he relaxed, he would miss something important, and that missing something would have consequences he could not undo. That belief left him feeling permanently changed for the worse, as though the man who had once been able to trust his surroundings had not survived the war in the same way his body had.

He also carried a painful sense that he would never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened. When he spoke about the traumatic event, his voice often narrowed around a few moments of helplessness and uncertainty, as if he kept returning to the point where action had been needed and he had not been able to provide it. The memory did not come to him as a vague blur. It came back in clear and detailed pieces, and he could still describe what he saw, what he heard, and even what he smelled when he thought about it. That clarity made it harder for him to set the event apart from the present. He no longer felt at ease in situations where he might be surprised, and he had started avoiding anything that made him feel too exposed or too keyed up, especially settings where aircraft sounds were likely.

His job as a park ranger, once a source of pride, became more complicated because the environment itself could place him directly in contact with those sounds. In the field, he might hear a helicopter during a rescue, search, or routine park operation and feel that old spike of alarm move through him. He kept working, but the effort of staying composed while monitoring the air, the trails, and the people around him was exhausting. At home, his wife saw how often he seemed braced for something to happen. He had become quieter about what he was carrying, but not less burdened by it. What finally brought Marcus to seek help was the growing strain of living as if danger were always nearby and of feeling stuck with the belief that he had been permanently altered by one night of combat. He came hoping for some relief from the sound-triggered surges of fear, the sense of unreality, and the relentless need to stay on guard, while fearing that if he did nothing, he would continue to live as a man waiting for the next threat and unable to make peace with what he believed he should have done.
